page.title: Does Rapid Trigger Still Work on a Hall Effect Keyboard in Wireless Mode?
page.h1: Does rapid trigger still work on a Hall effect keyboard in wireless mode?
page.desc: Yes on 2.4 GHz: one magnetic keyboard measured 0.75 ms wireless against 0.60 ms wired. Polling rate by connection for six boards, with prices read 2026-11-21.
page.answer: Short answer. Yes: rapid trigger still works on a Hall effect keyboard in wireless mode, and 2.4GHz keeps it close to wired. The Gamakay TK75 TMR magnetic keyboard measured 0.75 ms on 2.4GHz against 0.60 ms wired (HLPlanet); Bluetooth mode cuts polling to 1,000 Hz.

page.after:
What the differences mean

Polling rate sets the gap between reports to the PC. 1,000 ms ÷ 8,000 Hz = 0.125 ms. 1,000 ms ÷ 1,000 Hz = 1 ms. 1,000 ms ÷ 125 Hz = 8 ms. A board that holds 8,000 Hz on its 2.4 GHz dongle sends 8 reports in the time a 1,000 Hz board sends one, and 64 in the time a 125 Hz Bluetooth link sends one (8,000 ÷ 125).

On the pick, the measured cost of going wireless is small. Marcus Richardson at HLPlanet measured the Gamakay TK75 TMR at 0.60 ms wired and 0.75 ms on 2.4 GHz with OSLTT: 0.75 − 0.60 = 0.15 ms, or 25% more (0.15 ÷ 0.60). One frame on a 240 Hz monitor lasts 1,000 ÷ 240 = 4.17 ms, so 0.15 ms is about 4% of a frame. Bluetooth costs far more: HLPlanet's review of the Epomaker HE75 V2 TMR lists 15 ms on Bluetooth against 0.58 ms on 2.4 GHz, about 26 times as long (15 ÷ 0.58) and 3.6 frames at 240 Hz (15 ÷ 4.17).

Why the TK75 TMR is the pick when the Epomaker shows a lower 2.4 GHz number: the question is what you lose by unplugging, and the TK75 TMR loses 0.15 ms against the Epomaker's 0.48 ms (0.58 − 0.1). It also has two separate measurements. The two HLPlanet reviews have different authors and the Epomaker review names no test tool, so the 0.17 ms between the two boards on 2.4 GHz (0.75 − 0.58) is not a controlled comparison. During Gamakay's Black Friday sale (ends 2026-11-30) the TK75 TMR is {after:gamakay-tk75-tmr} through our link, below the Epomaker at $109.65 and the Keychron at $103.99 (both read 2026-11-21). The Aula Hero75 HE costs less at $83.03 and its listing states the same 8,000 Hz on 2.4 GHz; what it lacks among the pages we read is a named reviewer's wireless measurement. The TK75 TMR uses a TMR sensor, not a Hall sensor. It reads the same kind of magnetic switch and offers the same rapid trigger feature. If you want a Hall sensor specifically, the NS75 and TK75HE V2 rows are the ones to look at. Dealectric does not test units: every figure here is a maker's statement or a named reviewer's measurement, read on 2026-11-21.

Measured: wired against 2.4 GHz and Bluetooth

Rapid trigger is worked out inside the keyboard. Gamakay describes it this way: "This feature allows keys to be activated or deactivated based on their travel distance rather than a fixed point". The Aula listing says rapid trigger "adjusts activation and reset with key movement". The board reads each key's position (HLPlanet's spec table lists a 256,000 Hz scan rate for the TK75 TMR), decides press or release, then sends the result over whichever link is active. The link changes how often and how late that result arrives. It does not change where the key triggers. The maker and seller pages we read list rapid trigger and the wireless modes side by side and give polling by connection. None adds a sentence joining the two, and neither reviewer says rapid trigger was switched on during the 2.4 GHz test. So the evidence that it holds up on a dongle is the measured latency below.

BoardWired2.4 GHzBluetoothWho measured
Gamakay TK75 TMR0.60 ms0.75 ms1,000 Hz stated; no latency publishedHLPlanet (Marcus Richardson, 2026-05-18), OSLTT
Gamakay TK75 TMR0.602 ms0.99 ms, labelled "wireless"No separate figureVortex Gaming, OSLTCS; the page says both wired and wireless support 8,000 Hz
Epomaker HE75 V2 TMR0.1 ms0.58 ms15 ms in the spec list, 14 ms at 125 Hz in the textHLPlanet (Fang, 2026-09-27); no tool named

Vortex Gaming's gap is 0.99 − 0.602 = 0.388 ms, about 64% over wired (0.388 ÷ 0.602). Both TK75 TMR results sit inside the range Marcus Richardson gives in HLPlanet's Hall effect guide: "A 2.4 GHz dongle typically adds 20–100% latency and Bluetooth adds far more". Use Bluetooth for typing and for a second device. For rapid trigger in games, use the dongle or the cable.

Not recommended for wireless rapid trigger

Two listings look like wireless boards and are not. The Aula Hero 68 HE ($69.46 at aulatechstore.com, 2026-11-21) is USB-C only, with no 2.4 GHz or Bluetooth. The Gamakay x NaughShark NS68 is sold in a Wired version ($36.79) and a Tri-mode version ($39.99, both read 2026-11-21) on one product page; the Wired version has no radio, so pick Tri-mode if you want it off the cable. And on any board in the table, Bluetooth is the wrong mode for rapid trigger play: the Aula listing puts its Bluetooth rate at 125 Hz, which is one report every 8 ms.
